title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities, but the bar for clinical applications is high. Attempts to assess the clinical knowledge of models typically rely on automated evaluations based on limited benchmarks. Here, to address these limitations, we present MultiMedQA, a benchmark combining six existing medical question answering datasets spanning professional medicine, research and consumer queries and a new dataset of medical questions searched online, HealthSearchQA. We propose a human evaluation framework for model answers along multiple axes including factuality, comprehension, reasoning, possible harm and bias. In addition, we evaluate Pathways Language Model (PaLM, a 540-billion parameter LLM) and its instruction-tuned variant, Flan-PaLM on MultiMedQA. Using a combination of prompting strategies, Flan-PaLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on every MultiMedQA multiple-choice dataset (MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA and Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) clinical topics), including 67.6% accuracy on MedQA (US Medical Licensing Exam-style questions), surpassing the prior state of the art by more than 17%. However, human evaluation reveals key gaps. To resolve this, we introduce instruction prompt tuning, a parameter-efficient approach for aligning LLMs to new domains using a few exemplars. The resulting model, Med-PaLM, performs encouragingly, but remains inferior to clinicians. We show that comprehension, knowledge recall and reasoning improve with model scale and instruction prompt tuning, suggesting the potential utility of LLMs in medicine.
explain_beginner: The question, can a large language model, the same basic technology behind general purpose chatbots, actually answer medical exam style questions and open ended clinical questions accurately enough to be useful, or even safely, in medicine. Researchers cared because language models were improving fast on general tasks, but medicine has a much higher bar for being wrong, an answer that sounds fluent and confident but contains a factual error could mislead a patient or clinician, so they needed to test not just whether these models could answer medical questions but whether the answers were actually safe compared with those from real clinicians. The team built a broad medical question benchmark combining professional exam questions, research questions, and real consumer health searches, and found a large language model tuned for this task answered US medical licensing exam style questions correctly about two out of three times, comfortably beating the previous best model, and that with additional tuning aimed at safer long form answers, the rate of answers a human reviewer judged as potentially harmful dropped dramatically, down near the rate seen in answers written by actual clinicians. What it does not settle, the models were still tested mostly on curated exam style questions rather than messy real clinical conversations, and the authors are clear their models remained less reliable overall than clinicians.
explain_business: This paper is the technical proof point that large language models can approach, though not yet match, clinician level safety on written medical question answering, and it is the evidence base that later, more product oriented medical AI assistants were built on. The dramatic gap between the earlier model's 29.7 percent potentially harmful answer rate and the tuned model's 5.9 percent shows that model choice and specific safety tuning matter enormously, a generic large language model without this kind of medical safety tuning should be assumed to produce fluent but wrong answers at a meaningfully higher rate. A 67.6 percent score on licensing exam style questions is good enough to beat prior specialist medical models, but is not the same as being ready for autonomous clinical use, since the authors themselves stress multiple choice questions are easier than real practice. Nothing about this paper constitutes regulatory clearance, it is foundational research, so any product built on this line of work still needs its own separate clinical validation and approval pathway before deployment. This is relevant mainly to teams building or vetting medical question answering or documentation assistants, as a benchmark for what strong safety tuning can achieve.
explain_practitioner: Method, introduced the MultiMedQA benchmark, combining six existing medical question answering datasets spanning professional exams, biomedical research, and consumer queries, plus a newly created dataset of real world consumer health search questions, and evaluated Google's PaLM, an instruction tuned variant called Flan-PaLM, and a further instruction prompt tuned version called Med-PaLM. Flan-PaLM reached 67.6 percent accuracy on MedQA, the US Medical Licensing Exam style multiple choice benchmark, beating the prior best model, a 2.7 billion parameter system called PubMedGPT, by more than 17 percentage points. On human graded long form answers, Med-PaLM cut the rate of answers judged potentially harmful to 5.9 percent, down from 29.7 percent for the earlier Flan-PaLM version, approaching the 5.7 percent rate measured for answers written by actual clinicians, and Med-PaLM's rate of answers reflecting incorrect comprehension of the question fell to 2.1 percent versus 14.3 percent for Flan-PaLM. The authors state clear limitations, MultiMedQA, while broad, is not exhaustive, multiple choice question answering is inherently easier than real clinical workflows, the evaluation covered English language data only, their bias assessment was limited and not a comprehensive audit, and each answer in the human evaluation was judged by only a single clinician or layperson rather than multiple independent raters.
